There exists a close curve $C$ such that ${\int }_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s\ne 0$" :question/worked-solution "If $F=P\,i+Q\,j$ is a vector field with simply connected domain $D⊆{R}^{2},$ then the following are equivalent: - $F$ is a source-free vector field. - $∇\cdot F=\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y}=0.$ - The flux ${∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s$ along any closed curve $C⊂D$ is zero. - Flux is path-independent. That is, given any two curves ${C}_{1},{C}_{2}⊂D$ with the same start and endpoints, we have that $$ {\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s. $$ - There exists a stream function $ψ(x,y)$ for $F.$ Note that $F(x,y)={x}^{2}\,i+2x{y}^{2}\,j$ is a vector field with the simply connected domain $D={R}^{2},$ where $P(x,y)={x}^{2}$ and $Q(x,y)=2x{y}^{2}.$ Computing the partial derivatives, we have $$ \begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂x}=2x,\,\frac{∂Q}{∂y} & =4xy.\end{aligned} $$ With that in mind, let's consider each statement. - Statement I is false. Indeed, we have that $$ \frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y}=2x+4xy=2x(1+2y)\ne 0. $$ - Statement II is false, while statement III is true. Indeed, they follow from the fact that $∇\cdot F\ne 0.$ Therefore, the correct answer is "III only."" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields :question/worked-solution "If $F=P\,i+Q\,j$ is a vector field with simply connected domain $D⊆{R}^{2},$ then the following are equivalent: - $F$ is a source-free vector field. - $∇\cdot F=\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y}=0.$ - The flux ${∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s$ along any closed curve $C\in D$ is zero. - Flux is path-independent. That is, given any two curves ${C}_{1},{C}_{2}\in D$ with the same start and endpoints, we have that $$ {\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s. $$ - There exists a stream function $ψ(x,y)$ for $F.$ First, notice that $$ \frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y}=\frac{∂}{∂x}(2x+y)+\frac{∂}{∂y}(-2y)=2-2=0, $$ which shows that $F$ is a source-free vector field. Since $F$ is source-free, we know the flux of $F$ is independent of the path. In particular, as we have that $$ {\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot {n}_{1}\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot {n}_{2}\,\text{d}s, $$ where ${C}_{2}$ is the line segment $\overset{―}{AB}$ traversed from $A$ to $B,$ and ${n}_{2}$ is the unit normal to ${C}_{2},$ as shown below. ![](images/6b/6bb6e38f83006fa9874ca0020e4eb016ea8eed7fec79596e984b94a0f3853d75.png) Notice that both ${n}_{1}$ and ${n}_{2}$ are ${90}^{∘}$ clockwise rotations of their respective unit tangent vectors. To calculate the flux of $F$ across ${C}_{2},$ we will use the formula $$ {\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot {n}_{2}\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{C}_{2}}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x. $$ To apply the formula, - the curve should be parametrized as $r(t)$ for $t\in [a,b],$ and - the unit normal vector ${n}_{2}$ *must* be a ${90}^{∘}$ clockwise rotation of the unit normal tangent vector $T(t).$ We have the parametrization $$ r(t)=(-3t+2)\,i+(2t-1)\,j,\,t\in [0,1]. $$ Therefore, $$ \begin{aligned}P(x,y) & =2x+y=2(-3t+2)+(2t-1)=-4t+3, \\ Q(x,y) & =-2y=-2(2t-1)=-4t+2.\end{aligned} $$ Computing the derivatives of $x(t)$ and $y(t)$ along the curve, we get $$ \begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(-3t+2)=-3, \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2t-1)=2.\end{aligned} $$ We evaluate the flux integral as follows: $$ \begin{aligned}{\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot {n}_{2}\text{d}s & ={\int }_{{C}_{2}}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x \\ & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(P\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}-Q\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})\,\text{d}t \\ & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(-4t+3)\cdot (2)-(-4t+2)\cdot (-3)\,\text{d}t \\ & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(-8t+6)+(6-12t)\,\text{d}t \\ & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(12-20t)\,\text{d}t \\ & ={[12t-10{t}^{2}]}_{0}^{1} \\ & =(12-10) \\ & =2\end{aligned} $$ Finally, we conclude that $$ {\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot {n}_{1}\,\text{d}s=2. $$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-19bee987-1ec3-5c8c-ac5a-92a635a303b9"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id $\overset{―}{AB}$ traversed from $A$ to $B$ can be parametrized as* $$ r=(1-2t)\,i+(-1+2t)\,j,\,t\in [0,1]. $$" :question/worked-solution "If $F=P\,i+Q\,j$ is a vector field with simply connected domain $D⊆{R}^{2},$ then the following are equivalent: - $F$ is a source-free vector field. - $∇\cdot F=\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y}=0.$ - The flux ${∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s$ along any closed curve $C\in D$ is zero. - Flux is path-independent. That is, given any two curves ${C}_{1},{C}_{2}\in D$ with the same start and endpoints, we have that $$ {\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s. $$ - There exists a stream function $ψ(x,y)$ for $F.$ First, notice that $$ \frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y}=\frac{∂}{∂x}(x)+\frac{∂}{∂y}(1-y)=1-1=0, $$ which shows that $F$ is a source-free vector field. Since $F$ is source-free, we know the flux of $F$ is independent of the path. In particular, as we have that $$ {\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot {n}_{1}\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot {n}_{2}\,\text{d}s, $$ where ${C}_{2}$ is the line segment $\overset{―}{AB}$ traversed from $A$ to $B,$ and ${n}_{2}$ is the unit normal to ${C}_{2},$ as shown below. ![](images/e2/e22757cf7c4e2be17cb71e63c550aa39a10ee1dc5895c63acd5a45f0baa94623.png) Notice that both ${n}_{1}$ and ${n}_{2}$ are ${90}^{∘}$ clockwise rotations of their respective unit tangent vectors. To calculate the flux of $F$ across ${C}_{2},$ we will use the formula $$ {\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot {n}_{2}\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{C}_{2}}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x. $$ To apply the formula, - the curve should be parametrized as $r(t)$ for $t\in [a,b],$ and - the unit normal vector ${n}_{2}$ *must* be a ${90}^{∘}$ clockwise rotation of the unit normal tangent vector $T(t).$ We have the parametrization $$ r(t)=(1-2t)\,i+(-1+2t)\,j,\,t\in [0,1]. $$ Therefore, $$ \begin{aligned}P(x,y) & =x=1-2t, \\ Q(x,y) & =1-y=1-(2t-1)=2-2t.\end{aligned} $$ Computing the derivatives of $x(t)$ and $y(t)$ along the curve, we get $$ \begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(1-2t)=-2, \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2t-1)=2.\end{aligned} $$ We evaluate the flux integral as follows: $$ \begin{aligned}{\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot {n}_{2}\text{d}s & ={\int }_{{C}_{2}}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x \\ & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(P\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}-Q\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})\,\text{d}t \\ & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(1-2t)\cdot (2)-(2-2t)\cdot (-2)\,\text{d}t \\ & =2{\int }_{0}^{1}(1-2t)+(2-2t)\,\text{d}t \\ & =2{\int }_{0}^{1}3-4t\,\text{d}t \\ & =2\cdot {[3t-2{t}^{2}]}_{0}^{1} \\ & =2\cdot (3-2) \\ & =2\cdot 1 \\ & =2\end{aligned} $$ Finally, we conclude that $$ {\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot {n}_{1}\,\text{d}s=2. $$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186194303 :answer-field/correct 17592186194307 :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id 17592186199478 :tutorial/content "Consider the vector field $\mathbf F,$ given by $$ \mathbf F(x,y)= P(x,y)\,\mathbf{i} + Q(x,y)\,\mathbf{j} $$ which is defined on an open set $D\subseteq \mathbb R^2.$ Recall that a function $\psi(x,y)$ is said to be a **stream function** of $\mathbf F$ if it satisfies $$ P = \dfrac{\partial \psi}{\partial y}, \qquad Q = -\dfrac{\partial \psi}{\partial x}. $$ If a vector field $\mathbf{F}(x,y)$ has a stream function $\psi(x,y),$ then $\mathbf{F}$ is called a **source-free vector field**. Source-free vector fields have some interesting properties, summarized below: - *The divergence of $\mathbf{F}$ at any point of $D$ is zero:* $$ \textrm{div}\,\mathbf{F} = \nabla \cdot \mathbf F = \dfrac{\partial P}{\partial x} + \dfrac{\partial Q}{\partial y} = 0 $$ - *The *flux* of $\mathbf{F}$ along any closed curve $C \in D$ is zero:* $$ \oint\limits_C \mathbf{F} \cdot \mathbf{n} \,\textrm{d}s = 0 $$ - *Flux is path-independent. That is, given any two curves $C_1, C_2 \in D$ with the same start and endpoints, we have that* $$ \int\limits_{C_1} \mathbf{F} \cdot \mathbf{n} \,\textrm{d}s = \int\limits_{C_2} \mathbf{F} \cdot \mathbf{n} \,\textrm{d}s. $$ Stream functions for source-free vector fields play a similar role to potential functions for conservative vector fields. So it's worth comparing them side-by-side.
Source-Free
Stream Function $\psi$ $\mathbf F = \dfrac{\partial \psi}{\partial y}\,\mathbf i - \dfrac{\partial \psi}{\partial x}\,\mathbf j$
Relationship between $\psi$ and $\mathbf F$ $\mathbf F$ is tangential to $\psi$'s level curves
Divergence is zero $\dfrac{\partial P}{\partial x} + \dfrac{\partial Q}{\partial y} = 0$
Flux is zero along closed curves $\displaystyle\oint\limits_C \mathbf{F} \cdot \mathbf{n} \,\textrm{d}s = 0$
Flux integrals are path independent $\displaystyle\int\limits_{C_1} \mathbf{F} \cdot \mathbf{n} \,\textrm{d}s = \int\limits_{C_2} \mathbf{F} \cdot \mathbf{n} \,\textrm{d}s$
Conservative
Potential Function $\phi$ $\mathbf F = \dfrac{\partial \phi}{\partial x}\,\mathbf i + \dfrac{\partial \phi}{\partial y}\,\mathbf j$
Relationship between $\phi$ and $\mathbf F$ $\mathbf F$ is perpendicular to $\phi$'s level curves
(Scalar) curl is zero $\dfrac{\partial Q}{\partial x} - \dfrac{\partial P}{\partial y} = 0$
Circulation is zero along closed curves $\displaystyle\oint\limits_C \mathbf{F} \cdot \textrm d \mathbf{r}= 0$
Line integrals are path independent $\displaystyle\int\limits_{C_1} \mathbf{F} \cdot \textrm d \mathbf{r} = \int\limits_{C_2} \mathbf{F}\cdot \textrm d \mathbf{r}$
" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186199485 :tutorial/content "Let's use what we know about source-free vector fields to calculate the flux of $$ \mathbf{F}(x,y)=2y\,\mathbf{i}-2x\,\mathbf{j} $$ across the curve $C,$ shown below. ![](images/d6/d6adda2809af5d49c6b3dd0e81eae913dcdf02ceec0ae919fda0011d8a3dad2b.png) First, notice that this is a source-free vector field, since $$ \begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(2y)+\frac{∂}{∂y}(-2x) \\ & =0+0 \\ & =0.\end{aligned} $$ Therefore, since $\mathbf{F}$ is source-free, the flux of $\mathbf{F}$ across any closed curve is zero. Hence, $$ \oint\limits_{C} \mathbf{F} \cdot \mathbf{n} \,\textrm{d}s = 0. $$" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186198492 :activity/expected-seconds 600.0 :db/ensure [:activity/validate]}]

To calculate the flux of $F$ across ${C}_{2},$ we will use the formula $$ {\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot {n}_{2}\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{C}_{2}}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x. $$ To apply the formula, - the curve should be parametrized as $r(t)$ for $t\in [a,b],$ and - the unit normal vector ${n}_{2}$ *must* be a ${90}^{∘}$ clockwise rotation of the unit normal tangent vector $T(t).$ We have the parametrization $$ r(t)=(-3t+2)\,i+(2t-1)\,j,\,t\in [0,1]. $$ Therefore, $$ \begin{aligned}P(x,y) & =2x+y=2(-3t+2)+(2t-1)=-4t+3, \\ Q(x,y) & =-2y=-2(2t-1)=-4t+2.\end{aligned} $$ Computing the Source-free vector fields have some interesting properties, summarized below: - *The divergence of $\mathbf{F}$ at any point of $D$ is zero:* $$ \textrm{div}\,\mathbf{F} = \nabla \cdot \mathbf F = \dfrac{\partial P}{\partial x} + \dfrac{\partial Q}{\partial y} = 0 $$ - *The *flux* of $\mathbf{F}$ along any closed curve $C \in D$ is zero:* $$ \oint\limits_C \mathbf{F} \cdot \mathbf{n} \,\textrm{d}s = 0 $$ - *Flux is path-independent. That is, given any two curves $C_1, C_2 \in D$ with the same start and endpoints, we have that* $$ \int\limits_{C_1} \mathbf{F} \cdot \mathbf{n} \,\textrm{d}s = \int\limits_{C_2} \mathbf{F} \cdot \mathbf{n} \,\textrm{d}s. $$ Stream functions for source-free vector fields play a similar role to potential functions for conservative vector fields. So it's worth comparing them side-by-side.
Source-Free
Stream Function $\psi$ $\mathbf F = \dfrac{\partial \psi}{\partial y}\,\mathbf i - \dfrac{\partial \psi}{\partial x}\,\mathbf j$
Relationship between $\psi$ and $\mathbf F$ $\mathbf F$ is tangential to $\psi$'s level curves
Divergence is zero $\dfrac{\partial P}{\partial x} + \dfrac{\partial Q}{\partial y} = 0$
Flux is zero along closed curves $\displaystyle\oint\limits_C \mathbf{F} \cdot \mathbf{n} \,\textrm{d}s = 0$
Flux integrals are path independent $\displaystyle\int\limits_{C_1} \mathbf{F} \cdot \mathbf{n} \,\textrm{d}s = \int\limits_{C_2} \mathbf{F} \cdot \mathbf{n} \,\textrm{d}s$
Conservative
Potential Function $\phi$ $\mathbf F = \dfrac{\partial \phi}{\partial x}\,\mathbf i + \dfrac{\partial \phi}{\partial y}\,\mathbf j$
Relationship between $\phi$ and $\mathbf F$ $\mathbf F$ is perpendicular to $\phi$'s level curves
(Scalar) curl is zero $\dfrac{\partial Q}{\partial x} - \dfrac{\partial P}{\partial y} = 0$
Circulation is zero along closed curves $\displaystyle\oint\limits_C \mathbf{F} \cdot \textrm d \mathbf{r}= 0$
Line integrals are path independent $\displaystyle\int\limits_{C_1} \mathbf{F} \cdot \textrm d \mathbf{r} = \int\limits_{C_2} \mathbf{F}\cdot \textrm d \mathbf{r}$

The curve $C_1$ has endpoints $A(5,3)$ and $B(1,3).$ Calculate the flux of the vector field 

$$
\mathbf{F}(x,y)=\sqrt{y^3}\,\mathbf{i}+\sqrt{(5-x)^3}\,\mathbf{j}
$$

 through $C_1$ measured with respect to the unit normal vector  $\mathbf{n}_1,$ as shown above. 

*Hint: You're given that $\mathbf F$ is source-free.*" :question/worked-solution "If $\mathbf{F} = P\,\mathbf{i} + Q\,\mathbf{j}$ is a vector field with simply connected domain $D \subseteq \mathbb{R}^2,$ then the following are equivalent:

- $\mathbf{F}$ is a source-free vector field.

- $\nabla \cdot \mathbf F = \dfrac{\partial P}{\partial x} + \dfrac{\partial Q}{\partial y} = 0.$

- The flux $\displaystyle{\oint\limits_C \mathbf{F} \cdot \mathbf{n} \,\textrm{d}s}$ along any closed curve $C \in D$ is zero.

- Flux is path-independent. That is, given any two curves $C_1, C_2 \in D$ with the same start and endpoints, we have that

$$
\int\limits_{C_1} \mathbf{F} \cdot \mathbf{n}  \,\textrm{d}s
=
\int\limits_{C_2} \mathbf{F} \cdot \mathbf{n}  \,\textrm{d}s.
$$

- There exists a stream function $\psi(x,y)$ for $\mathbf{F}.$

First, notice that

$$
\dfrac{\partial P}{\partial x} + \dfrac{\partial Q}{\partial y} = \dfrac{\partial}{\partial x}\left(\sqrt{y^3}\right) + \dfrac{\partial}{\partial y}\left(\sqrt{(5-x)^3}\right) = 0+0 = 0,
$$

which shows that $\mathbf{F}$ is a source-free vector field.

Since $\mathbf{F}$ is source-free, we know the flux of $\mathbf{F}$ is independent of the path. In particular,

$$
\int\limits_{C_1} \mathbf{F} \cdot \mathbf{n}_1 \,\textrm{d}s
=
\int\limits_{C_2} \mathbf{F} \cdot \mathbf{n}_2 \,\textrm{d}s,
$$

where $C_2$ is the straight line from $A(5,3)$ to $B(1,3)$ and $\mathbf{n}_2$ is its unit normal, shown in the diagram below. 

![](images/2a/2aeb26e58251923821d4058f886eada6a29b473ea70714b32e98c5338ddd0b28.png)

Notice that both $\mathbf n_1$ and $\mathbf n_2$ are $90^\circ$ clockwise rotations of their respective unit tangent vectors.

To calculate the flux of $\mathbf F$ across $C_2,$ we will use the formula

$$
\int\limits_{C_2} \mathbf{F} \cdot \mathbf{n}_2 \,\textrm{d}s  = \int\limits_{C_2} P\,\textrm{d}y - Q\,\textrm{d}x.
$$

To apply the formula,

- the curve should be parametrized as $\mathbf{r}(t)$ for $t \in [a,b],$ and

- the unit normal vector $\mathbf{n}_2$ *must* be a $90^\circ$ clockwise rotation of the unit normal tangent vector $\mathbf{T}(t).$

Parametrizing $C_2,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =5\,i+3\,j+t\cdot [(i+3\,j)-(5\,i+3\,j)] \\  & =(5-4t)\,i+3\,j\end{aligned}
$$

where $t\in [0,1].$ Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(x,y) & =\sqrt{{y}^{3}}=\sqrt{(3)^{3}}=3\sqrt{3}, \\ Q(x,y) & =\sqrt{(5-x)^{3}}=\sqrt{(5-(5-4t))^{3}}=8\sqrt{{t}^{3}}.\end{aligned}
$$

 

Computing the derivatives of $x(t)$ and $y(t)$ along the curve, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(5-4t)=-4, \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3)=0.\end{aligned}
$$

We evaluate the flux integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot {n}_{2}\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{{C}_{2}}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(P\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}-Q\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(3\sqrt{3})\cdot (0)-(8\sqrt{{t}^{3}})\cdot (-4)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}32{t}^{3/2}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={[\frac{64{t}^{5/2}}{5}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =(\frac{64(1)^{5/2}}{5})-(\frac{(64(0)^{5/2}}{5}) \\  & =\frac{64}{5}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we conclude that

$$
\int\limits_{C_1} \mathbf{F} \cdot \mathbf{n}_1\, \textrm{d}s = \dfrac{64}{5}.
$$"} {:db/id 17592186050793} {:db/id 17592186198612 :question/id #uuid "bdff88fa-fe4d-5059-a512-6bd7bc96d899" :question/math-academy-id "q-161439" :knowledge-point/_questions [{:db/id 17592186198403 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "fd9aad0a-f415-577c-9cb0-15044e4a43fa" :knowledge-point/title "Calculating Flux in a Source-Free Vector Field"}] :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "b20b10fc-bb64-57ca-9ec9-e4d2df501a0f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "1" :db/id 17592186194304} {:answer/id #uuid "c439e078-219a-5d7c-931d-f4512f82a95f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "\frac{1}{2}" :db/id 17592186194305} {:answer/id #uuid "c5449f6b-066e-5959-8004-2b1d283f4af0" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "0" :db/id 17592186194306} {:answer/id #uuid "f048743c-1904-5a19-bb5a-ec041bc93630" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "2" :db/id 17592186194307} {:answer/id #uuid "36e11e32-f25b-529c-abe5-51889402664c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "-2" :db/id 17592186194308}] :answer-field/id #uuid "7d966562-9c87-57b1-a8bf-6b3edf2422f8" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493 :db/ident :answer-field.type/radio} :db/id 17592186194303}] :question/problem "![](images/07/07aaf788552b002f804b98558a79a2951ac091897539093bbffc0063a2289897.png)

:tutorial/content "Consider the vector field $\mathbf F,$ given by

$$\mathbf F(x,y)= P(x,y)\,\mathbf{i} + Q(x,y)\,\mathbf{j}$$

which is defined on an open set $D\subseteq \mathbb R^2.$ Recall that a function $\psi(x,y)$ is said to be a **stream function** of $\mathbf F$ if it satisfies

$$P = \dfrac{\partial \psi}{\partial y}, \qquad Q = -\dfrac{\partial \psi}{\partial x}.$$

If a vector field $\mathbf{F}(x,y)$ has a stream function $\psi(x,y),$ then $\mathbf{F}$ is called a **source-free vector field**.

Source-free vector fields have some interesting properties, summarized below:

- *The divergence of $\mathbf{F}$ at any point of $D$ is zero:* $$\textrm{div}\,\mathbf{F} = \nabla \cdot \mathbf F = \dfrac{\partial P}{\partial x} + \dfrac{\partial Q}{\partial y} = 0$$
- *The*flux*of $\mathbf{F}$ along any closed curve $C \in D$ is zero:* $$\oint\limits_C \mathbf{F} \cdot \mathbf{n} \,\textrm{d}s = 0$$
- *Flux is path-independent. That is, given any two curves $C_1, C_2 \in D$ with the same start and endpoints, we have that* $$\int\limits_{C_1} \mathbf{F} \cdot \mathbf{n} \,\textrm{d}s = \int\limits_{C_2} \mathbf{F} \cdot \mathbf{n} \,\textrm{d}s.$$

Stream functions for source-free vector fields play a similar role to potential functions for conservative vector fields. So it's worth comparing them side-by-side.

$$\mathbf F(x,y)= P(x,y)\,\mathbf{i} + Q(x,y)\,\mathbf{j}$$

which is defined on an open set $D\subseteq \mathbb R^2.$ Recall that a function $\psi(x,y)$ is said to be a **stream function** of $\mathbf F$ if it satisfies

$$P = \dfrac{\partial \psi}{\partial y}, \qquad Q = -\dfrac{\partial \psi}{\partial x}.$$

If a vector field $\mathbf{F}(x,y)$ has a stream function $\psi(x,y),$ then $\mathbf{F}$ is called a **source-free vector field**.

Source-free vector fields have some interesting properties, summarized below:

- *The divergence of $\mathbf{F}$ at any point of $D$ is zero:* $$\textrm{div}\,\mathbf{F} = \nabla \cdot \mathbf F = \dfrac{\partial P}{\partial x} + \dfrac{\partial Q}{\partial y} = 0$$
- *The*flux*of $\mathbf{F}$ along any closed curve $C \in D$ is zero:* $$\oint\limits_C \mathbf{F} \cdot \mathbf{n} \,\textrm{d}s = 0$$
- *Flux is path-independent. That is, given any two curves $C_1, C_2 \in D$ with the same start and endpoints, we have that* $$\int\limits_{C_1} \mathbf{F} \cdot \mathbf{n} \,\textrm{d}s = \int\limits_{C_2} \mathbf{F} \cdot \mathbf{n} \,\textrm{d}s.$$

Stream functions for source-free vector fields play a similar role to potential functions for conservative vector fields. So it's worth comparing them side-by-side.

These techniques allow physicists to compute quantities such as mass distributions, charge densities, and gravitational or electric potentials.

Applications of multivariable calculus follow, including vector mechanics and optimization.
